story_v1.post:
A long eCom ad only works when every section has a job.

When I hand clients a long draft, the first reaction is often "WOAH, this copy is LONG!" That reaction is fine. What loses the reader is a section that repeats the one before it.

Here is the order I'd check on any ad going to cold traffic:

→ An opening that fits how aware the reader already is
→ The problem, in the words customers use in their reviews
→ A clear picture of their day with the product in it
→ Why it works, in plain language, with proof
→ The one objection that stops the click, answered
→ The offer and an honest reason to act now

If a part is missing, that's usually where the reader drops off. If two parts do the same job, cut one and make the other better.

Your current ad might be a one-liner that works on people who already know you. Put it next to this list and you'll see what a stranger still needs to hear.

The long-copy ad checklist kit puts this check into Claude. Paste your draft in and it marks each part as present, weak or missing.

story_v1.email:
Hi Alex,

One check in the kit is worth doing first: the objection section.

A lot of eCom ads go straight from benefits to the offer. A cold reader still has one doubt in their head, and if the ad never answers it, they keep scrolling.

Here's how to find that doubt. Search your reviews for "at first", "I was worried", "almost didn't" and "I thought". Those lines usually hold the worry a buyer had before they bought.

For example, say a kitchen brand sells a cast iron skillet for $60 and has 400 reviews. The phrases that keep coming up might be "I thought it would be too heavy" and "I was worried about rust". That's your objection section: one or two sentences that name the worry in those same words, then show how the product handles it.

After you add it, run the checklist skill again. If it still marks the objection as weak, the answer is probably too vague. Show it instead: a hand lifting the pan, a quick wipe after cooking.

Omar
Nabil Advertising

skills.body:
# Long-copy ad checklist

You check one eCom paid social ad against a one-page long-copy checklist and return that checklist filled in for this ad.

## Ask first
- The ad text: primary text, headline, any video script.
- The product, price and who it is for.
- Where it runs: cold, warm or retargeting.
- The markets the brand sells into.
If the traffic type is missing, ask. Cold traffic changes every judgement below.

## Steps
1. Name the awareness stage the opening is written for: Unaware, Problem-aware, Solution-aware, Product-aware or Most aware. Compare it with the traffic type. A cold ad that opens with the brand name or a discount is written for Most aware readers. Flag it.
2. Mark each part Present, Weak or Missing:
   - Opening that earns the next line for this stage
   - Problem in the customer's own words
   - Picture of the day with the product in it
   - Mechanism: why it works, in plain words
   - Proof: reviews, demo, numbers with a source
   - Biggest objection, named and answered
   - Offer and an honest reason to act now
3. For each Weak or Missing part, quote the closest line and say what it needs. Do not rewrite the whole ad.
4. Flag any section that repeats the job of the one before it. Repetition is what makes long copy boring.
5. Run the claims check below.

## Judgement calls
- On cold traffic, a one-line ad usually skips problem, mechanism and objection. Say so plainly.
- Brand-speak test: if a line could sit on any competitor's ad, mark it Weak.
- Proof must be checkable. "Thousands love it" with no source is Weak.
- Urgency must be true. A countdown or "almost gone" with no real limit is treated as misleading in many markets. Mark it as a risk.
- Lead with benefits, and back them with one concrete fact about how the product works.

## Claims check
If the product is a supplement, food, skincare, medical device, or touches health, weight or money, mark every health, weight or financial claim Restricted. These claims are regulated, so never treat them as a matter of tone. Tell the user to check the current rule with the regulator in each market they sell into (for example the US, UK, Canada, EU or GCC countries) and Meta's advertising standards before running the ad. Never suggest stronger claim wording.

## Output
Long-copy ad checklist: [product]
Traffic: ... | Opening written for: ... | Match: Yes or No
Table: Part | Status | Closest line | What it needs
Repeats: ...
Claims check: ...
Fix first: the one change that matters most, in one sentence.

skills.body:
# Review angle miner

You turn raw customer words into a bank of ad angles for an eCom product.

## Ask first
- The reviews, support emails or comments. 50 or more is best, including 2 and 3 star ones.
- The product, price and the markets they sell into.
- What their live ads currently say, in a line or two.

## Steps
1. Pull exact phrases word for word. Never paraphrase a customer and present it as a quote.
2. Sort each phrase into one reason to buy: Problem, Desire, Mechanism, Proof, Objection or Identity.
3. Group phrases into themes and count mentions. A theme with 3 or more mentions is a strong candidate. Keep a single quote too if it paints a vivid scene.
4. Compare the themes with the live ads. Mark each theme Running or Untested.
5. For the top 3 untested themes, write one hook line built from the customer's own words and name the awareness stage it suits.

## Judgement calls
- 2 and 3 star reviews hold the objections. Lines with "at first", "I was worried", "almost didn't" or "I thought" feed the objection section of an ad.
- Keep specific phrases like "cleans up in a minute". Drop praise with no detail, like "great product".
- Ignore one-off delivery complaints unless they form a pattern.
- If a theme appears only in the brand's own wording and never in customer words, label it a brand belief.
- Health, weight, skin or money results in reviews are claims. A customer may write them, but a brand repeating them in an ad is restricted in most markets. Mark them Restricted and tell the user to check the current rule with the regulator in each market they sell into and Meta's advertising standards before using them.
- Quoting a named review in an ad may need the customer's permission and the review platform's terms. Flag it.

## Output
Table: Reason | Theme | Exact quotes (up to 3) | Mentions | Running or Untested
Top 3 untested angles: each with stage, hook line and the quotes it came from.
Restricted claims found: list them, or say none.

skills.body:
# Awareness stage map

You map a brand's live ads so the user can see which awareness stages and reasons to buy are covered and where the gaps are.

## Ask first
- Each live ad: first line or hook, format (UGC, talking head, static, demo, founder story, testimonial and so on) and rough share of spend if known.
- Whether the budget is mostly cold, warm or retargeting.
- The product and the main customer.

## Steps
1. Tag each ad with one awareness stage, using Eugene Schwartz's five: Unaware, Problem-aware, Solution-aware, Product-aware, Most aware. Judge by the opening line, since that decides who keeps reading.
2. Tag each ad with one reason to buy: Problem, Desire, Mechanism, Proof, Objection, Identity.
3. Group ads that share stage and reason into one concept. A new visual, creator or first three words on the same promise is a variation of that concept.
4. Build a grid of stage by reason and place each concept in it with its spend share.
5. Pick the 2 or 3 empty cells most worth briefing next and write one line on each.

## Judgement calls
- If one concept holds more than half the spend, call it a concentration risk: when it tires, nothing else is ready.
- Cold budget with mostly Product-aware or Most aware openings means the ads speak to people who already know the brand. Flag this first.
- No Problem-aware ad at all is usually the first gap to fill for cold traffic.
- Unaware ads need more copy and a stronger story. Suggest them when buyers do not see the problem yet.
- Most aware ads (offer, discount, proof) suit retargeting and rarely introduce new buyers.
- You cannot see results. Do not guess which ad performs. Ask the user if it matters for a decision.

## Output
1. Table: Ad | Stage | Reason | Format | Concept number
2. Grid: stages down the side, reasons across the top, concept numbers and spend share in the cells
3. Gaps to brief: 2 or 3 lines, each naming stage, reason and a format that fits
4. One sentence on the biggest risk in the current mix

skills.body:
# New angle brief for a tired winner

You help the user replace a fading winning ad with a new reason to buy, and write a brief their creators or editors can shoot.

## Ask first
- The winning ad's script or copy, and its format.
- How long it has run and what changed, in their words (click rate, frequency, cost per purchase).
- Any recent change to offer, price, landing page or budget.
- Customer reviews or notes.
- Who produces the ad: in-house team, creators or editors.

## Steps
1. Name why the winner works in one line: its awareness stage, its reason to buy and its hook.
2. Check it is fatigue. Rising frequency with a falling click rate on the same audience points that way. If results dropped right after an offer, page or budget change, say it may be that change and suggest checking it first.
3. List 3 reasons to buy the winner does not use, each backed by a review quote or a product fact.
4. Pick the strongest one and say why in one sentence.
5. Write the brief.

## Judgement calls
- A new creator, colour or first line on the same promise is an iteration. Label it so it is not tested as a new angle.
- One idea per brief. Two promises in one ad make the test hard to read.
- Keep the winner's proof if it still fits the new reason.
- Write hooks a creator can say out loud in the first 3 seconds.
- Any health, weight, skin or money claim is restricted: mark it, and tell the user to check the current rule with the regulator in each market they sell into and Meta's advertising standards.

## Output
Why the winner works: one line
Fatigue check: one or two lines
Three unused reasons: each with its evidence
Brief
- Audience and stage
- Reason to buy
- Hooks: 3 options
- Body beats: 4 to 6 lines
- Proof to show
- Objection to answer
- Format and creator direction
- What the test should tell us

story_v1.plainPost:
When a winning ad starts to tire, 20 more versions of the same hook won't bring it back.

Meta's delivery system does more of the audience finding now. The ad itself does a big part of the targeting. If every new ad gives the same reason to buy, it keeps reaching people who have already heard that argument.

A new color, a new creator or new first three words still carry the same argument.

So before you brief the next batch, write down the one reason your winner works. Then look for the other reasons people buy your product:

→ Problem: the pain they want gone
→ Desire: the result they're after
→ Mechanism: why this works when other things didn't
→ Proof: what makes them believe it
→ Objection: the doubt that stops them
→ Identity: the kind of person who owns it

Each one can carry its own ad.

Your reviews already tell you which reasons your customers care about. Read the 3-star ones too. That's where the doubts are written out in full.

Brief one new reason at a time and give your media buyer something different to test.
